In modern philosophy, examples include Malebranche (1638–1715), Berkeley (1685–1753), and David Hume (1711–1776).
Malebranche explained the relationship between body and soul in much the same way that he explained two clocks showing the same time: God moves both clocks together at every moment.
In Malebranche’s view, then, there is no necessary connection in the universe and no true cause within it.
There is only one real cause: God.
This divine presence in the actions of created things closely resembles the Ashʿarite idea of continuous renewed creation.

Berkeley explains causal relationships between the phenomena of existence from the same subjective idealist position. He says that the pain I feel when I touch fire is not caused by the fire itself. Rather, the cause is a divine sign warning me that pain may follow. He then asks: Why are pain and burning always associated with fire? His answer is that this happens because God acts according to fixed and lasting rules. We call these rules laws of nature, but in reality they are God’s laws.

The problem of causality also plays a major role in Hume’s philosophy. He asks, for example: What is the causal relationship between events? Or what is necessity? Hume answers that when we repeatedly observe two events occurring together and following one another, we become used to expecting the same pattern every time. From this, he concludes that the only reality we can be certain of is the repeated succession of two perceptions. This repetition creates in us a firm expectation that the same sequence will continue. We call this expectation a “law.” Imagination also plays a part here, and what imagination adds is what we call “causality.” Hume later goes on to argue that the law of causality has only a hypothetical character.

The partial similarity between the Ashʿarites and philosophers of this kind in the way they explain relationships between events in the universe comes, in turn, from a partial similarity in their subjective idealist and metaphysical positions. From everything discussed above, we can finally conclude that the Ashʿarites—above all al-Ghazālī—came close to the position later taken by Hume: that the necessity we observe between cause and effect is only an empirical necessity, not a logical one.
6 — The Name “Logic” and Its Theoretical Meaning

The fact that this science is called manṭiq in Arabic points to a sound understanding of the relationship between the linguistic meaning of the Arabic word and its intellectual meaning. In one way or another, those who chose this Arabic name must have understood the basic ontological and dialectical relationship between language and thought.
Language is the spoken form of thought, while thought is the content that language expresses through that form. Because of this, language and thought affect one another in a dialectical process.

This does not mean, however, that there was no connection between the Arabic name manṭiq and the name of the same science that originally came from Greek, Logic. Those who chose the Arabic term may well have known the derivation of the word Logic: that it came from Logiche, meaning speech, which in turn was derived from the Greek word Logos, meaning “the core and essence of thought.”

So we cannot rule out the possibility that the Arabic name was inspired by this Greek derivation. But that does not mean Arab thinkers were unaware of how precisely the term, in both languages, expressed the ontological and dialectical relationship between thought and language. Quite the opposite. Arab writings on logic show that they understood this relationship deeply.
There are several signs of this.

First, they explicitly discussed this relationship in their works on logic. The fullest, clearest and most precise statement of it, in our view, comes from Abū Naṣr al-Fārābī. In a chapter devoted to logic, he explains that the subjects of this science are:
“The concepts of the mind insofar as words point to them, and words insofar as they point to those concepts.”
Elsewhere in the same discussion he says:

“For this reason, we need rules that protect us both in our concepts and in the way we express them, and that guard us against error in both. The ancients called both of these—that is, the concepts and the statements through which they are expressed—‘logic and speech.’ They called the concepts ‘speech’ and ‘inner logic rooted in the soul,’ while the speech through which they are expressed is ‘outer logic voiced aloud.’ What enables a person to correct an opinion within himself is the speech rooted in the soul, while what enables him to correct it in another person is speech expressed aloud. The ancients called any speech whose purpose is to establish the correctness of an opinion a ‘syllogism,’ whether that speech remained within the soul or was expressed aloud.”
We have quoted this passage at length because it shows, with unusual clarity and precision, how deeply al-Fārābī understood the relationship between thought and language.

Abū Ḥayyān al-Tawḥīdī also has an interesting discussion of the relationship between logic and grammar, which is itself one form of the relationship between thought and language. In it he gives this brief and striking formulation:
“Grammar is Arabic logic, and logic is rational grammar.”
Second, Arab logicians added new discussions to Aristotle’s logic in the section dealing with concepts. They called these “discussions of words.”

They understood a concept, in the logical sense, as the mind’s grasp of a single term. Since that single term is expressed through a word, they began to study words in terms of the meanings they convey, rather than simply as words in themselves.

This gave rise to a whole set of discussions about language that went beyond what was found in Aristotle’s logic. In Arabic works on logic, the study of concepts therefore became richer through a variety of classifications of words, reflecting the different relationships involved in expression.

Words were classified according to how they signify meaning, according to how general or specific their meaning is, according to whether they are single or compound, according to the word itself, according to its relationship with its meaning, and in several other ways.

At first sight, these discussions may seem purely linguistic. But Arab logicians gave them a logical character as well. They did so because, as we said earlier, they had a sound understanding of the real dialectical relationship between thought and language.

We therefore find here another Arab-Islamic response to Aristotle’s logic. This time it was a constructive one. Arab thinkers developed some of the relationships between words already present in Aristotelian logic and enriched logic with new areas of study.

At the same time, these developments opened new theoretical possibilities for Arab-Islamic disciplines such as the principles of Islamic law, kalām, Qurʾānic interpretation, grammar, philology and rhetoric.
Logic has been closely tied to philosophy for a very long time.

We can already see the beginnings of this connection in Plato’s philosophical classifications, which had an early logical character. It continued with the birth of Aristotle’s logic within his philosophical system, then with the appearance of the Isagoge in the setting of Neoplatonism.

Logic and philosophy later reappeared together as Arab-Islamic thought developed in the Middle Ages. They then continued to change together through the great scientific transformations of the European Renaissance and the modern period, until the rise of Marxist philosophy and its dialectical logic.
This historical connection has a theoretical basis in the nature of both logic and philosophy.

Philosophy, as we all know, is the highest form of abstraction. It is, in fact, the language of concepts—concepts understood as universals or essences. But we cannot speak in the language of concepts, which is the language of abstraction, without using categories, and categories stand at the center of the study of logic.

Categories are simply expressions of species and genera arranged according to increasing degrees of generality. We move upward until we reach the highest genus: the most general and inclusive form of being.
Categories, then, are existing things expressed as abstract concepts or universals—that is, as species and genera.

Aristotle, the father of logic, held that there were ten highest genera. These were his ten categories. At their head, and serving as the point of reference for the others, stood the category of substance. Substance was also the central subject of Aristotle’s Metaphysics, or what he called “first philosophy.”
The other nine categories were quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, state, action and being acted upon.

Aristotle treated these categories as general and universal conceptual features of things that form part of what those things are. In other words, he treated them as species or genera of existing things.
For this reason, Aristotle sometimes calls the categories “kinds of being” and also “general genera” (Summa general).

This way of understanding the categories gives them real content and shows that they are originally connected with things that exist outside the mind. In that sense, they have a material significance.
Arab logicians and philosophers approached the categories on the same basis and in the same spirit.

We can see this from the disagreement among them over whether the categories belonged to logic or to metaphysics. In practice, this disagreement had little effect on how they treated their content. Almost all of them discussed the categories within logic, even those who believed that the subject also had a metaphysical side.

Ibn Sīnā himself believed that the categories properly belonged to metaphysics, yet he still included them in the logic section of al-Shifāʾ. In fact, his discussion of the nature of judgments, or logical categories, is one of the most valuable parts of his work.
More broadly, much of the importance of Ibn Sīnā’s logic comes from the fact that he dealt with the content of logical categories, one of the most difficult problems in philosophy.
Since Aristotle, one of the central problems of both logic and philosophy had been the structure of concepts, judgments and conclusions.
Ibn Sīnā begins above all with the problem of judgment. He sees a judgment as establishing a connection between two things, and this is itself a logical category.

A judgment therefore determines a particular subject. When we want to determine what a subject is, we first identify the genus to which it belongs and then add the characteristics that distinguish the individual thing. The genus through which we identify the subject is itself a logical category.
Judgments can therefore be classified according to the logical category on which they are based.
Ibn Sīnā accepts ten categories, just as Aristotle does. For that reason, he distinguishes ten types of judgment, since every judgment rests on a logical category.

Among these are the definitive judgment, which is based on the category of essence; the hypothetical judgment, which is based on the category of cause; and the certain judgment, which is based on the category of necessity.

Ibn Rushd, by contrast, never hesitated over whether the categories belonged to logic rather than metaphysics. He placed them in his discussion of Aristotle’s logic, not in his discussion of Aristotle’s metaphysics, and treated them purely as logical categories.

Only later Muslim logicians and theologians removed the categories from the heart of logic. These were thinkers with conservative, traditionalist tendencies who tried to strip Aristotelian logic of its concern with content and confine it to purely formal reasoning, as Ibn Khaldūn later pointed out.
Plotinus, however, also had a system of ten categories, presented in the seventh section of the Enneads. He arranged them differently, in a way that reflected the idealist outlook of Neoplatonism.
He divided them into two groups.
The first consisted of five categories belonging to the intelligible world. The second consisted of five belonging to the sensory world.
The first five were substance, rest, motion, identity and difference (L’identité et la différence).
The second five were substance, relation, quantity, motion and quality.
Plotinus then reduced the last three of these to relation.
Did Arab logicians, theologians or philosophers come under the influence of this Plotinian classification?

We have no source that clearly says so. The only relevant evidence we know of comes from al-Tahānawī, who reports that some thinkers reduced the categories to four: substance, quantity, quality and relation—or possession—which they believed included the remaining seven categories of the traditional ten.
He also says that “the slain shaykh,” meaning al-Suhrawardī, “made them five by treating motion as a category in its own right.”
Neither of these later classifications, however, gives us clear evidence that their authors were following Plotinus in limiting the number of categories.
Aristotle’s logic relies on demonstration as the way to acquire knowledge.
He recognizes two kinds: syllogism and induction. Aristotle calls the first syllogistic, or deductive, demonstration, and the second inductive demonstration.
In his view, the difference is that the first gives scientific certainty, while the second gives only probable knowledge.
The reason is that a demonstrative syllogism reaches knowledge by relying on first principles of reason. These first principles cannot themselves be demonstrated because they are self-evident.
Inductive demonstration, by contrast, begins with individual cases and moves from them to the universal that includes them all, meaning the essence they are all understood to share.
For Aristotle, induction can be scientifically certain only if it is complete—that is, only if it includes every individual case before reaching the general law that covers them.
But it is impossible to include every case. Induction therefore remains incomplete, and incomplete induction cannot produce certainty.
Aristotle built his entire logical system around the problem of how demonstration is constructed.
He first concluded that demonstrations must be made up of propositions. He then concluded that propositions are made up of words or terms.

He therefore organized the general structure of logic around two basic areas. The first was the study of terms, which he called the study of concepts. The second was the study of propositions made up of those terms, which he called the study of judgments.
In his discussion of propositions, however, Aristotle dealt only with categorical propositions. He did not examine conditional propositions, whether connected or disjunctive.
The study of definition was also part of the foundation of Aristotle’s logical system because it served the same ultimate aim as demonstration: acquiring knowledge.
For Aristotle, definition is one of the ways we reach knowledge because it allows us to understand the essence of things.
This is the basic outline of demonstration in Aristotle’s logic. We have presented it here as a starting point for examining the changes it underwent among medieval Arab thinkers.
The first thing that stands out is how much they expanded the study of syllogism beyond what we find in Aristotle.
This expansion appeared in two main areas.
First, in their treatment of propositions.
Second, in their treatment of the different figures of the syllogism.

In the case of propositions, Arab logicians discussed not only categorical propositions but also different kinds of conditional propositions. Here they benefited from additions made by later Greek commentators on Aristotle’s logic, especially Alexander of Aphrodisias and Porphyry of Tyre, the author of the Isagoge.

As for the figures of the syllogism, Arab logicians also discussed a fourth figure. Aristotle had either ignored this figure or had at least not stated it explicitly, since his attention was limited to the first three.
In the fourth figure discussed by Arab logicians, the middle term is the subject in the minor premise and the predicate in the major premise.
Ibn Rushd attributes the invention of this fourth figure to Galen after Aristotle.

But the fact that Arab logicians discussed the fourth figure does not mean that they actually used it in demonstrative syllogisms, that they regarded it as equal in value to the other three, or that they all took the same position toward it.
Some, including Ibn Sīnā and al-Sāwī, discussed the fourth figure but explicitly said that they did not rely on it because it was “remote from natural reasoning.”

Al-Ghazālī mentioned it when classifying syllogisms according to the position of the middle term. But when he turned to the figures produced by this classification, he did not discuss the fourth figure at all. This effectively meant that he rejected it as a method of reasoning.
Later Arab logicians, however, gave the fourth figure much more attention and added new forms of it that there is no need to discuss here in detail.
Arab thinkers treated inductive demonstration on an essentially Aristotelian basis, without changing it.

They regarded induction as a probable form of demonstration that could not produce certainty. Their reason was the same as Aristotle’s: complete induction is impossible, while incomplete induction is not enough to give certain knowledge.
Aristotle also treated analogy as a method of reasoning. Arab thinkers adopted the idea as well, although they did not agree either on how to understand it or on how much value to give it.

Reasoning by analogy means moving from one particular case to another particular case. It is defined as “giving one particular case the same judgment as another particular case because the two share a common feature.”
Ibn Sīnā, however, does not justify the judgment simply by treating the similar case as an “original” and the new case as a “branch,” as others do.
Instead, he bases the judgment on the “common feature,” which he identifies as “the cause or the sign”—in other words, on the cause shared by both cases.

Here Ibn Sīnā rejects the idea that analogy works simply through formal comparison and instead grounds it in causality. In this, he was influenced by Shīʿī legal thought, since Shīʿī jurisprudence does not accept qiyās, or legal analogy.
Theologians and scholars of legal theory, meanwhile, used a principle they called “reasoning from the seen to the unseen.”
